description: CircaLuna es una aplicación web de salud para astronautas que cuida su reloj biológico (ritmo circadiano). En el espacio no hay amaneceres de 24 horas, y eso daña el sueño, la atención y aumenta el riesgo de errores. El astronauta registra en menos de un minuto cuándo durmió, cuánta luz recibió y qué tan alerta estuvo. La app calcula su reloj interno y le indica cuándo exponerse a luz intensa, cuándo realizar tareas delicadas y cómo adaptarse a cambios de turno.
summary:
CircaLuna is an app that estimates an astronaut's body clock from their sleep schedule and the light they receive, then prescribes each day exactly when to take bright light. It aims to reduce circadian misalignment on space missions and improve sleep, alertness and performance. It works offline, without internet access.


 CircaLuna is an app that calculates each astronaut's body clock and prescribes the light needed to keep it on time. The astronaut logs when they sleep and what light they get at three moments of the day; a mathematical model of the circadian rhythm estimates their internal phase, shows whether they run early or late, and recommends when to get bright light. It also shows a traffic light with the best hours for delicate tasks and a plan to spread shift changes gradually over several days.

It answers the astronaut health challenge with a tool that does not just record, but decides: it turns simple data into a concrete action. It works offline, which is key far from Earth, and adapts to scenarios such as the ISS, Mars (a 24 h 39 min sol) and the Moon. In simulations, the plan reduces misalignment after a shift change.

 Poor sleep degrades attention and health, and in a mission mistakes are costly. The same tool could help people on night shifts on Earth. It is an educational simulation, not a medical device, and it still needs validation with real astronaut data.
details:
CircaLuna is an offline web app that keeps an astronaut's body clock aligned with their mission schedule. Each day, the astronaut logs when they woke up, when they slept, and the light they received during three parts of their waking hours (start, middle, end): dark, indoor, very bright or direct sun. A simplified circadian model, inspired by the Kronauer and Forger models, estimates whether the internal clock runs early or late. If the gap exceeds one hour, CircaLuna prescribes two to three hours of strong light, timed to advance or delay the clock. It also shows a traffic-light bar with the best hours for delicate tasks and splits planned schedule changes into steps of at most 1.5 hours per day.

Benefits

Astronauts get a concrete action instead of raw data. The app works without internet, keeps data on the device, needs no special hardware, and explains its recommendation with a clock dial.

Expected impact

In my synthetic simulations, a five-hour ISS schedule change peaked at about 4.9 hours of misalignment, versus about 2.1 hours with the gradual plan and light prescriptions. These are stylized simulations, not evidence about real people. The same engine could help night-shift workers and people in polar regions. Next step: validation with published data and real wearable recordings.

Tools and technologies

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, Canvas API, inline SVG and localStorage, with no external libraries. I used Node.js for headless tests and Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, to help write and review code and text. The project does not yet use NASA datasets directly.

What makes it creative

Existing efforts measure light and sleep or provide a few fixed lighting presets. CircaLuna is the missing brain between them: it turns measurements into a personalized prescription, handles non-24-hour days such as a Martian sol, plans shift changes gradually, and works offline.

Factors I considered

As a solo participant with limited time, I focused on one problem and a usable prototype. I considered safety (an educational tool, not a medical device), privacy (local data), connectivity (offline use), and usability on phones. Limitations: a simplified model, coarse light categories, an approximate camera, stylized scenarios, and no real astronaut data.
